summary: Berkshire Hathaway Inc.’s 2025 Form 10-K cover identifies the company, fiscal year, incorporation, headquarters, contact details, NYSE-listed common shares and senior notes, and confirms no Section 12(g) securities. It reports filer status, filing and internal-control certifications, market value and shares outstanding, and proxy materials incorporated by reference. The contents list covers business, risks, cybersecurity, properties, legal matters, market and operating results, financial statements and notes, controls, governance, compensation, ownership, related transactions, auditors, exhibits, and signatures.

title: Part I

nodes.title: Item 1. Business Description
nodes.summary: Berkshire Hathaway is a Delaware holding company headquartered in Omaha, with major insurance, rail, utility and energy businesses plus manufacturing, service and retail operations. Its subsidiaries operate under a highly decentralized structure; the CEO oversees capital allocation, investments and operating performance, while corporate management monitors governance and the Board selects the CEO’s successor. Its ethics code sets standards for lawful and ethical conduct. At year-end 2025, Berkshire employed about 387,800 people worldwide (80% in the U.S.; 19% unionized). Subsidiaries set their own workforce policies, commonly covering safety, compensation and benefits, wellness, training and advancement, and hiring. Combined U.S. workforce data is available on its website.

nodes.title: Insurance Businesses
Insurance Businesses (intro)
nodes.summary: Berkshire’s global insurance subsidiaries provide property-casualty, life, health and reinsurance coverage and employed about 42,600 people in 2025. The text explains primary insurance and reinsurance, competition, and U.S. regulation of admitted and surplus-lines insurers, including NAIC standards and international IAIS frameworks, group supervision, capital tools and Berkshire’s supervisory college. It reports Berkshire’s $333 billion U.S. statutory surplus and strong ratings; describes TRIA terrorism coverage, eligibility, reimbursement, deductibles and limits; and outlines foreign regulation and operations. It defines underwriting profit and introduces GEICO’s products, sales channels, competitors, market share, risks, regulation, pricing, claims handling and trademarks.

nodes.title: GEICO
nodes.summary: The text explains TRIA eligibility, exclusions, reimbursement, deductibles and program limits; variation in foreign insurance regulation and Berkshire’s international operations; underwriting-profit expectations and the three insurance groups. It describes GEICO’s products, distribution, competition, market share, risks and regulation; BH Primary’s insurers, lines, locations and sales channels; and BHRG’s global structure and treaty/facultative, quota-share/excess-of-loss arrangements. It details property/casualty and life/health reinsurance businesses, including major relationships and markets, and explains retroactive reinsurance, its long-tail claims, investment-float rationale and lack of recent significant contracts.

nodes.title: Reinsurance Business and Market Conditions
nodes.summary: Business volumes across the three BHRG groups fluctuate with market conditions, pricing adequacy and large transactions. Property/casualty operations describe NICO’s reinsurance and specialty insurance, including its IAG quota share through 2029; General Re’s North American and international treaty, facultative and specialty business; and TransRe’s global broker-led reinsurance. General Re and BHLN also write life and health reinsurance, including variable-annuity risks in runoff. Retroactive reinsurance covers prior-year claims, potentially including asbestos and environmental losses; long-tail payments make investment returns important despite expected underwriting losses, and no significant contracts have been written recently.

nodes.title: Periodic payment annuity
nodes.summary: BHLN’s periodic-payment annuities fund long-term structured settlements, with premiums generally below ultimate payments; it stopped issuing policies in 2022. Berkshire’s insurance investments include concentrated public equities, short-term and fixed-maturity securities, and policyholder float, which grew from about $138 billion in 2020 to $176 billion in 2025; float cost is measured by underwriting results relative to average float. BNSF operates a large North American freight railway, serving varied regions and industries through routes, shortlines, and carrier agreements. Revenues and performance depend on contracts, prices, competition, product supply and demand, and economic conditions. Federal, state, and Canadian regulators oversee its rates, routes, services, rail-line transactions, safety, health, and environmental operations, including hazardous-material transport.

Covers Berkshire’s insurance operations, workforce, primary and reinsurance models, competition, U.S. and international regulation, capital and ratings, terrorism coverage, and underwriting profit. Describes GEICO, BH Primary and BHRG, their products, markets, distribution, risks, and property-casualty, life and health reinsurance, including retroactive contracts, long-tail claims and periodic-payment annuities. Also discusses insurance investments and float, then BNSF’s freight network, business drivers, competition and extensive federal, state and Canadian regulation.

nodes.title: Burlington Northern Santa Fe
nodes.summary: BHLN’s periodic-payment annuities fund long-term structured settlements, generally produce underwriting losses because future payments exceed upfront premiums, and have not been newly written since 2022. The text explains Berkshire insurance investments, concentrated equity holdings, float and its growth from about $138 billion in 2020 to $176 billion in 2025, and float cost. It describes BNSF’s rail operations, workforce, routes, freight categories, revenue arrangements, economic and competitive pressures, regulatory oversight, environmental liabilities, and emissions-reduction plans. It also introduces BHE’s diversified energy and real-estate businesses, customer and pipeline scale, workforce, and U.S. utility subsidiaries.

nodes.title: Berkshire Hathaway Energy
Energy businesses
nodes.summary: The text describes BNSF’s environmental regulatory exposure, cleanup and third-party liabilities, hazardous-material risks, and plans to reduce greenhouse gas emissions through fuel efficiency, renewable diesel, and evaluation of battery-electric and hydrogen locomotives. It outlines rail competition from carriers, other transport modes, and Union Pacific, and the pursuit of operating efficiencies. It then surveys Berkshire Hathaway Energy’s businesses, workforce, customers, utilities, generation capacity and seasonal patterns; interstate gas pipelines and storage/LNG operations; electricity distribution in Great Britain and transmission in Alberta; and renewable independent power projects and tax-equity investments.

nodes.title: Regulatory matters
nodes.summary: U.S. utilities face extensive federal, state and local oversight. FERC regulates wholesale electricity rates, transmission, reliability, utility holding companies, records, securities, hydropower and enforcement; MEC is also subject to nuclear regulation for its Quad Cities ownership. Utilities generally have exclusive retail service territories and service obligations, with some customer choice or self-generation; state commissions set cost-of-service rates intended to recover reasonable costs and provide fair returns, including bundled and unbundled service options. UK Northern Powergrid distribution charges are formula-controlled for 2023–2028. Alberta’s AUC regulates AltaLink’s tariffs and operations, while AESO runs the grid and wholesale market. FERC regulates named interstate gas pipelines and facilities; federal pipeline-safety rules govern their design, construction, operation and maintenance.

nodes.title: Environmental matters
nodes.summary: BHE’s operations face extensive environmental laws and penalties, including air-quality rules that may require plant emission reductions and potential clean-energy standards. The text reviews the Paris Agreement and U.S. withdrawals and reentry; EPA’s 2026 repeal of the GHG Endangerment Finding and anticipated litigation; 2024 power-sector GHG rules, proposed rescission, and methane rules, challenges, and delayed deadlines. BHE reports $38 billion invested in renewables and storage, 22 coal-unit closures, and a 30% emissions reduction from 2005 by 2025, and plans further customer-focused, reliable, cost-effective low-carbon investment and coal closures.

nodes.title: Non-Energy businesses
nodes.summary: HomeServices of America is a U.S. residential real estate brokerage offering brokerage, mortgage, title and closing, insurance, home warranty, relocation, and other home-related services. It operates nearly 35,000 agents across 770-plus offices in 35 states and D.C. under 46 brands. Its franchise network has over 250 franchisees, nearly 1,400 offices, and about 39,700 agents using two brands; services include brand rights, training, consultation, and advertising. Revenue depends on transaction volumes, typically higher in the second and third quarters, and the business faces strong competition and broader real estate market conditions.

The section covers BNSF’s environmental and hazardous-material liabilities, emissions-reduction efforts, rail competition and efficiency initiatives; Berkshire Hathaway Energy’s utilities, gas pipelines, electricity distribution, generation, renewable projects and tax-equity investments; extensive U.S., UK and Alberta utility and pipeline regulation; environmental laws, climate rules, emissions progress and plans for reliable, lower-carbon energy; and HomeServices of America’s real estate, mortgage, title, insurance, franchise and related businesses, footprint, seasonal revenue patterns and competitive and market conditions.

nodes.title: Manufacturing Businesses
Industrial products
nodes.summary: Berkshire’s manufacturing businesses employ about 175,600 people and span industrial, building and consumer products. The text details industrial subsidiaries and their products, markets, operations, customers, competition, raw-material supply, risks, regulation and environmental commitments. It covers Precision Castparts’ aerospace, energy and industrial components; Lubrizol’s specialty chemicals and materials; IMC’s carbide cutting tools; Marmon’s diverse manufacturing, service, railcar, leasing, crane and medical groups; and other businesses in agricultural systems, pipeline drag reduction, structural steel and rodent control. It also describes OxyChem, acquired in January 2026, its chlor-alkali and PVC operations, feedstocks, markets, customers and regulatory obligations.

nodes.title: Building products
nodes.summary: The text profiles Berkshire Hathaway’s building-products businesses: Clayton’s off-site and site-built homes, sales and financing, backlogs, inputs, affordability factors, environmental compliance and lending regulation; Shaw’s flooring, turf, geosynthetics and services, global operations, distribution, materials, competition and pricing; Johns Manville’s insulation, roofing and specialty products, markets, facilities, materials, environmental regulation, competition and seasonality; MiTek’s residential and commercial building products and steel inputs; Benjamin Moore’s coatings, brands, retail and online channels, competition, materials and environmental obligations; and Acme’s brick, block and distributed products, operations, seasonality, raw materials and compliance with air-emission standards.

nodes.title: Consumer products
nodes.summary: The text surveys Berkshire’s consumer businesses. Forest River makes RVs, trailers, trucks, buses and pontoon boats, describes its brands, dealer network, manufacturing footprint, competitive position and safety regulation. Apparel and footwear operations cover Fruit of the Loom’s products, brands, production, sourcing, raw materials and competition; Garan’s children’s clothing and channels; Fechheimer’s public-service uniforms; BH Shoe’s footwear; and Brooks running products, including overseas sourcing and sales channels. Other businesses include Duracell batteries and market share, Jazwares toys and licensed products, Richline jewelry and related materials for varied markets, and Larson-Juhl custom framing products and services.

Covers Berkshire’s manufacturing businesses and roughly 175,600 employees across industrial, building and consumer products. Profiles subsidiaries, products, markets, operations, customers and distribution, competition, sourcing and raw materials, seasonality, and relevant risks and regulations. Industrial operations include aerospace components, chemicals, cutting tools, railcars and other products; building businesses span homes, flooring, insulation, construction products, coatings and masonry; consumer businesses make vehicles and boats, apparel and footwear, batteries, toys, jewelry and custom framing.

nodes.title: Service and Retailing Businesses
nodes.summary: Describes Berkshire’s service and retail businesses, their operations, scale, locations, products, customers, staffing, competition, and regulatory considerations. Service businesses cover NetJets aviation solutions, FlightSafety training and simulators, TTI electronic-component distribution, McLane wholesale distribution, and other transportation leasing, engineering, restaurant franchising, media, furniture rental, broadcasting, and logistics operations. Retailing covers automotive dealerships and related services, home-furnishings chains, Pilot travel centers and fuel businesses, jewelry retailers, See’s confectionery, Pampered Chef, Oriental Trading, and Louis motorcycle retail. It identifies sources for segment and investment financial details and explains how to access Berkshire and SEC reports. The risk-factor section notes unknown or immaterial risks may also matter, and highlights terrorism threats and cybersecurity attacks, including potential operational, financial, safety, compliance, information-security, and reputational harms.

It introduces business risks, noting that terrorist attacks could cause casualties, facility or information-system destruction, property damage, and significant losses to worldwide operations.

nodes.title: Cybersecurity risks could result in economic losses to our businesses and reputational damage.
nodes.summary: The text outlines risks from increasingly frequent and sophisticated cyberattacks, including operational disruption, information or asset loss, costs, reputational harm, regulatory issues, and adverse effects on finances, liquidity, and access to capital, despite mitigation planning; inability to adopt or protect new technology may also weaken competitiveness. Geopolitical conflict, government responses, sanctions, trade barriers, supply-chain disruption, property damage, and employee harm may hurt operations and securities values. Berkshire depends on key leaders, including CEO-designate Gregory Abel, and qualified managers and workers; succession planning mitigates leadership risk, while staffing shortages or labor disputes could impair results. Concentrated equity investments may lose value, reducing earnings, shareholder equity, insurers’ statutory surplus, ratings, insurance capacity, and future underwriting profits.

nodes.title: Operational, Geopolitical, Leadership, and Investment Risks
key_items: Geopolitical events could cause losses to our business and losses in the values of securities we own.
We are dependent on a few key people for our major investment and capital allocation decisions.
We need qualified personnel to manage and operate our various businesses.
Investments are unusually concentrated in equity securities and fair values are subject to loss in value.
nodes.summary: The page describes risks from operational disruptions, cyberattacks, technology challenges, and geopolitical conflict, including effects on business continuity, markets, supply chains, financing, and securities values. It notes reliance on key leaders for investment and capital allocation, succession planning, and the need to recruit and retain qualified managers and staff, with labor disruptions posing additional risks. Concentrated equity investments expose earnings, shareholders’ equity, insurers’ statutory surplus, ratings, and future underwriting capacity to declines in fair value.

nodes.title: Business Risks and Potential Impacts
key_items: Competition and technology may erode our business franchises and result in lower earnings.
Unfavorable general economic conditions may significantly reduce our operating earnings and impair our ability to access capital markets at a reasonable cost.
Epidemics, pandemics or other similar outbreaks could hurt our operating businesses.
Regulatory changes may adversely impact our future operating results.
Climate change and the regulation of greenhouse gas (“GHG”) emissions may impact our businesses.
nodes.summary: The page outlines risks that could reduce earnings or harm operations: competition, technological disruption, and intellectual-property challenges; economic downturns and inflation, including restricted or more costly capital-market access; epidemics and pandemics disrupting operations, supply chains, demand, customer payments, and investments; regulatory changes that raise compliance costs or create penalties, including rules on finance, products, environment, taxes, data privacy, and AI; and climate change, extreme weather, and GHG policies that may damage assets, generate insurance losses, increase compliance costs, or adversely affect financial results.

nodes.title: Risks unique to our regulated businesses Our tolerance for underwriting risk assumed in our various insurance businesses may result in significant underwriting losses.
nodes.summary: The company’s willingness to assume substantial insurance risk could produce major catastrophe losses, despite underwriting controls and efforts to limit single-event exposure; exclusions may be overturned or restricted, and losses may reduce future earnings. Claims can take decades to settle, making unpaid-loss estimates and premium adequacy uncertain, with past policies potentially generating unexpected claims. Evolving legal, social, and environmental conditions—including litigation funding, social inflation, and larger jury awards—may expand coverage and costs long after contracts are issued. Estimated unpaid property and casualty losses were $151.8 billion at year-end 2025, so even a small increase could materially reduce earnings.

nodes.title: Changes in regulations and regulatory actions can adversely affect our operating results and our ability to allocate capital.
nodes.summary: Regulatory changes and enforcement may restrict Berkshire’s insurance businesses—including underwriting, rates, capital, investments and dividends—and impair results or capital allocation. BNSF faces extensive rail regulation, compliance costs, litigation, potential policy-driven declines in coal and other freight, hazardous-material liabilities, limits on pricing and investment, and disruptions from interconnected transportation networks or industry consolidation. BHE’s complex utility and energy regulation can constrain operations, rates, financing and distributions; environmental rule changes, wildfire losses, and unrecoverable costs may materially harm results. BNSF and BHE require substantial, long-lived infrastructure investment, whose failures or costs may not be recoverable through rates; reliance on debt and restricted market access could weaken liquidity and capital resources.

nodes.title: Item 1C. Cybersecurity
nodes.summary: Berkshire’s cybersecurity framework lets business groups tailor risk controls while supporting consistent reporting. CISOs report annually on programs and material risks; groups report significant incidents, monitor third-party risks, and use external cybersecurity partners. The Audit Committee oversees the program, incident trends, and internal audit work, including penetration tests and vulnerability reviews; business-group management handles daily protection, while Berkshire management assesses SEC reporting. The properties section describes BNSF’s 32,500-plus route miles across the U.S. and Canada, track, facilities, equipment, and 2025 maintenance costs, and BHE’s electricity and natural-gas assets, associated rights, and debt-related encumbrances.

nodes.title: Cybersecurity Oversight and BNSF Properties
nodes.summary: Berkshire and its business groups rely on third-party providers, creating cyber risks they monitor. The Audit Committee oversees cybersecurity through incident and trend reports and internal audit plans covering testing, assessments, and reviews; business-group leaders manage daily protection, report significant events, and senior management assesses SEC reporting. The properties section notes the physical assets used by business segments. BNSF operates more than 32,500 route miles across 28 states and three Canadian provinces, with over 50,000 total track miles, extensive rail facilities, equipment, and transfer hubs. It owns or leases about 6,700 locomotives and 70,700 freight cars and spent approximately $2.4 billion on repairs and maintenance in 2025.

nodes.title: Berkshire Hathaway Energy
nodes.summary: BHE’s physical energy assets support electricity and natural-gas operations, include related rights and coal-mining assets, and are mostly pledged as debt security. The text lists operating generation technologies, subsidiaries, locations, facility and owned capacities, and capacity definitions; it also reports generation and battery-storage projects under construction. It describes electric transmission, distribution and gas-distribution networks, plus the pipeline, storage and LNG facilities of BHE GT&S, Northern Natural and Kern River, and the electricity networks of Northern Powergrid and AltaLink.

nodes.title: Business Properties, Legal Proceedings, and Mine Safety
nodes.summary: Summarizes property locations, types, and owned or leased counts across Berkshire’s other business segments. Describes routine and other pending litigation, including insurance-related claims and possible punitive damages, and states that such matters are not expected to materially affect financial condition or results. Refers readers to Note 27 for certain litigation details and Exhibit 95 for mine-safety disclosures under the Dodd-Frank Act.

nodes.title: Executive Officers of the Registrant
nodes.summary: The text lists Berkshire’s named executive officers through December 31, 2025, with their ages, positions, and service-start years: Warren E. Buffett (95, Chairman and CEO; 1970), Gregory E. Abel (63, Vice Chairman—Non-Insurance Operations; 2018), Ajit Jain (74, Vice Chairman—Insurance Operations; 2018), and Marc D. Hamburg (76, Senior Vice-President and CFO; 1992). Officers serve until the specified post-annual-meeting board meeting and a qualified successor, or earlier death, resignation, removal, or disqualification. title: FORWARD-LOOKING STATEMENTS

nodes.title: Forward-Looking Statements and Shareholder Information
nodes.summary: Explains that forward-looking statements are based on current expectations, are not guarantees, may not be updated, and can differ materially from actual results due to investment-price changes, disasters, outbreaks, regulatory or tax changes, and economic or market conditions. Berkshire’s Class A and B shares trade on the NYSE as BRK.A and BRK.B. As of February 13, 2026, it had about 950 Class A and 16,500 Class B record holders, with nominees holding shares for beneficial owners. Berkshire has paid no cash dividend since 1967.

nodes.title: Stock Repurchases and Performance Comparison
nodes.summary: Berkshire’s 2025 repurchase program allows its CEO, after consulting the Chairman, to buy Class A or B shares when their price is conservatively judged below intrinsic value, through market or private transactions; none were repurchased in the fourth quarter. The program has no share or dollar cap or expiration date, but repurchases cannot reduce cash, cash equivalents, and Treasury bills below $30 billion. A performance graph compares $100 invested in Berkshire from December 31, 2020, with the S&P 500 and Property & Casualty Insurance Index, using dividend-reinvested index returns; Berkshire notes that comparable companies are difficult to identify. Item 6 is reserved.

nodes.title: Item 7. Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations Results of Operations
nodes.summary: Berkshire reports net earnings by business for 2023–2025, totaling $67.0 billion, $89.0 billion and $96.2 billion, respectively, and directs readers to segment disclosures. It warns that geopolitical, trade and tariff uncertainty could affect operations, investments, supply chains and demand. Insurance underwriting earnings fell in 2025 but remained exceptional historically; catastrophe losses and future competitive and claims-cost pressures are noted. Insurance investment income declined in 2025 after rising in 2024. BNSF earnings rose in 2025 after a slight 2024 decline. BHE earnings increased in both years, with wildfire accruals, litigation and business performance among the factors. Manufacturing, service and retail earnings rose in 2025 after declining in 2024, with mixed results across businesses.

nodes.title: Results of Operations
nodes.summary: Discusses investment volatility, the 2023 Pilot remeasurement gain, 2025 Kraft Heinz and Occidental impairments, and lower 2025 other earnings. Summarizes insurance underwriting results and catastrophe-loss volatility, then details GEICO, BH Primary and BHRG operations and 2025 versus 2024 and 2024 versus 2023 performance. Covers premiums, losses and LAE, underwriting expenses and ratios, catastrophe losses, claims frequency and severity, prior-year reserve development, business mix, rate and volume changes, competitive pressures, and segment-specific drivers; includes underwriting tables and insurer descriptions.

nodes.title: BHRG
Property/casualty
nodes.summary: Insurance underwriting results compare 2024 with 2023 and BHRG property/casualty results for 2025, 2024 and 2023. In 2024, premiums written rose 3.8%, while losses and LAE and underwriting expenses increased, reflecting catastrophe losses, less favorable prior-year development, business mix and GUARD underwriting changes. BHRG provides global property/casualty, life/health, retroactive reinsurance and annuity coverage. Its 2025 property/casualty premiums fell amid competition and lower rates; losses and expenses declined, with catastrophe losses, favorable prior-year claims reductions, currency effects and a 2024 settlement charge noted. For 2024, premiums written fell but earned premiums rose; losses and loss ratio declined, while expenses rose, including the settlement charge. Tables report premiums, losses, expenses and pre-tax earnings.

nodes.title: Life/health
nodes.summary: The text reports life/health reinsurance results for 2023–2025, including written and earned premiums, benefits, expenses, and pre-tax underwriting earnings. In 2025, earned premiums rose $271 million (5.4%), mainly from non-U.S. markets, and earnings increased $151 million due to stronger international and U.S. business, lower U.S. long-term-care losses, and currency gains. In 2024, earned premiums fell $74 million, including the effect of 2023 contract commutations; excluding that effect, they declined $235 million (4.5%), mainly from non-U.S. life. Earnings fell $131 million, reflecting lower non-U.S. life earnings and higher run-off long-term-care losses, partly offset by U.S. life gains; commutation gains were $53 million in 2024 versus $134 million in 2023.

nodes.title: Insurance Underwriting and Investment Income
nodes.summary: Reviews retroactive reinsurance losses, liability increases, foreign-exchange effects, unpaid claims and deferred charges; periodic payment annuity losses, liabilities and currency effects; and variable annuity reinsurance earnings and market sensitivities. Reports insurance investment income by category, taxes and effective rates for 2023–2025, explaining changes in interest and dividend income, the impact of capital distributions to Berkshire, and the emphasis on liquidity and safety over yield.

nodes.title: Insurance—Investment Income
nodes.summary: The discussion explains insurance float, including its components and exclusions, and reports float of $176 billion in 2025, $171 billion in 2024 and $169 billion in 2023. Insurance operations earned pre-tax underwriting gains each year, making average float cost negative. It summarizes insurance cash and investments for 2025 and 2024, and 2025 fixed-maturity investments by category, amortized cost, unrealized gains and carrying value. U.S. government obligations were rated AA+/Aa1; about 95% of foreign government obligations were rated AA or higher.

Reviews BHRG’s property/casualty and life/health underwriting results for 2023–2025, including premiums, losses, expenses, earnings, catastrophe impacts, prior-year claims development, business mix, competition, commutations, and currency effects. Covers retroactive reinsurance, periodic-payment annuities, variable-annuity reinsurance, related liabilities and market sensitivities, and insurance investment income, taxes, and the effects of capital distributions. Explains insurance float and its negative average cost, reports cash and investments, and details fixed-maturity holdings, valuations, and government-obligation credit ratings.

nodes.title: BNSF
nodes.summary: BNSF operates over 32,500 route miles across 28 U.S. states and three Canadian provinces, serving consumer, industrial, agricultural and energy, and coal markets. The text reports 2023–2025 earnings in millions: revenues, operating expenses and earnings, other revenues and expenses, interest, pretax earnings, income taxes, net earnings, effective tax rates, and percentage changes. In 2025, net earnings were $5.476 billion and the effective tax rate was 23.7%.

title: BNSF

nodes.title: BNSF (intro)
nodes.summary: The discussion reviews BNSF freight volumes by business group for 2023–2025 and compares operating results across 2025–2024 and 2024–2023. It explains revenue, volume, pricing, expense, operating-ratio, earnings and tax changes, including labor-agreement, litigation, fuel, productivity and market factors. It describes BHE’s businesses and regulated-rate framework, presents earnings by year and segment, and discusses tax credits, the 2025 OBBBA and potential future effects. Segment analysis covers utilities, pipelines, other energy, real estate brokerage and corporate items, including wildfire accruals, margins, customer volumes, costs, acquisitions, litigation and housing-market conditions.

nodes.title: Manufacturing, Service and Retailing
Manufacturing, Service and Retailing (intro)
nodes.summary: The text reports 2023–2025 revenues, pre-tax earnings, net earnings, effective tax rates, and pre-tax margins for manufacturing, service and retailing, with year-over-year percentage changes. It notes that net earnings exclude specified acquisition-accounting expenses, gives their amounts and where they are reported, and describes manufacturing’s industrial, building, and consumer products businesses. For each manufacturing category, it presents revenues, pre-tax earnings, margins, and changes across the three years.

nodes.title: Industrial products
nodes.summary: The industrial products group spans aerospace, power and industrial components, specialty chemicals, metalworking, diversified manufacturing and leasing, agriculture, pipeline additives, steel fabrication, and—starting August 2025—rodent control; OxyChem was acquired January 2, 2026, with results consolidated from that date. In 2025, group revenue rose 4.1%, pretax earnings 13.1%, and margin 1.5 percentage points, though raw-material constraints may hurt 2026. PCC revenue and earnings grew on aerospace demand, efficiency, mix, and fire-related insurance recoveries; Lubrizol revenue and earnings fell due to prices, volumes, costs, restructuring, and litigation. Marmon revenue and earnings increased overall, with gains across several groups offset by declines, impairment, restructuring, and medical costs. IMC revenue rose on pricing, acquisitions, and mix, while earnings were flat amid higher costs; Israeli operations were not significantly affected by regional conflict. In 2024, group revenue and earnings rose 2.7% and 5.8%, respectively. PCC grew strongly on aerospace and power demand and improved operations; Lubrizol earnings rebounded despite flat revenue; Marmon revenue and earnings declined amid weaker businesses, partly offset by gains elsewhere; and IMC revenue and earnings fell due to lower organic sales, currency effects, and costs, partly offset by acquisitions and investment income.

nodes.title: Building products
nodes.summary: The text reviews Berkshire’s building and consumer products groups in 2025 versus 2024 and 2024 versus 2023. Building products include Clayton Homes and home-related manufacturers. In 2025, group revenue rose slightly but pretax earnings fell amid weaker demand and pricing; Clayton revenue grew while earnings were flat, and other businesses saw lower sales and earnings. In 2024, revenue rose and earnings dipped; Clayton revenue grew but earnings declined, while other businesses’ revenue fell and earnings improved. Consumer products include vehicles, apparel, footwear, batteries, toys, jewelry and framing. In 2025, revenue fell but reported earnings rose due to Duracell tax credits, while underlying earnings declined; in 2024, both revenue and earnings increased, led by apparel, footwear and Duracell.

nodes.title: Consumer products
nodes.summary: The text reviews 2024 performance of other building-products businesses and 2025-versus-2024 and 2024-versus-2023 results for consumer products, service, McLane and retailing. It details segment businesses, revenues, pretax earnings and margins, and their drivers: sales volumes, prices, mix, acquisitions, costs, efficiencies, restructuring, supply-chain disruption, demand, inflation, and operating expenses. It also describes Duracell’s retroactive production tax credits and Pilot’s reporting-period caveat. Retailing’s 2025 revenue rose while earnings fell, with NFM the exception to generally flat or lower earnings.

nodes.title: McLane
nodes.summary: In 2024, Service group revenue rose slightly to $20.7 billion as aviation services and IPS growth offset declines at TTI and XTRA; pre-tax earnings fell 23%, with lower TTI sales and margins, higher aviation costs and impairments, and weaker XTRA results. McLane, a low-margin wholesale distributor serving retail, restaurant and beverage customers, reported lower revenue but higher earnings in both 2025 and 2024, for differing reasons including fiscal-year length, volumes, inflation, sales mix and improved margins. Retailing includes auto, home-furnishing, jewelry, food, kitchenware, party-supply and motorcycle businesses; 2025 revenue increased 2.5% to $19.7 billion, while earnings fell 4.2%, with most businesses flat or down except NFM.

nodes.title: Retailing
nodes.summary: The text reviews 2024 and 2025 performance across service, McLane, retailing and Pilot. Service revenue rose slightly in 2024 as aviation and IPS gains offset declines at TTI and XTRA; earnings fell due to weaker sales and margins, higher operating costs and impairments. McLane revenue declined in both years, while pre-tax earnings increased, driven by improved margins in 2024 and stronger retail results in 2025. Retailing revenue rose in 2025 but earnings fell; BHA grew revenue modestly, while other retailers faced weak demand and lower margins. In 2024, retail revenue and earnings declined broadly. Pilot revenue and earnings fell sharply in both years, reflecting fuel volume, price and margin pressures, higher costs, and, in 2025, balance-sheet adjustments; reduced borrowing lowered interest expense. The text also describes McLane, retailing and Pilot operations and reports Pilot borrowings.

nodes.title: Pilot
nodes.summary: BHA’s 2025 revenue rose 4.2%, while pretax earnings edged down; other retail businesses saw lower revenue and earnings amid weak demand, competition, margin pressure and restructuring. In 2024, retail revenue and pretax earnings declined, with broad sales and margin weakness. Pilot revenue and pretax earnings fell sharply in both 2025 and 2024, driven by fuel prices, volumes and margins, alongside higher costs; its borrowing and 2024 refinancing are noted. Investment gains, taxes, net earnings and effective tax rates are reported for 2023–2025. Equity-market movements drove large unrealized gains, while realized gains, taxable sales and Pilot’s 2023 acquisition-accounting gain are detailed. The company cautions that investment gains and losses have limited analytical or predictive value.

nodes.title: GEICO
Berkshire Hathaway Reinsurance Group
nodes.summary: The text discusses critical estimates for unpaid property and casualty insurance losses. GEICO reports $27.5 billion gross and $26.6 billion net claim liabilities, estimated using claim frequency, severity and actuarial methods; 2025 reserve releases increased pretax earnings by $957 million, while a 1% BI severity change could move liabilities and earnings by $290 million. BHRG reports property and casualty unpaid losses and LAE, explaining the varied, delayed and sometimes incomplete cedent data, coverage allocation and dispute controls, and its use of case reviews and actuarial methods including development, Bornhuetter-Ferguson, frequency-severity and contract-level analyses. Its case estimates exceeded cedent estimates by $1.1 billion. BHRG reduced pre-2025 reserves by $1.1 billion in 2025, mainly from favorable property experience, partly offset by casualty increases. Portfolio diversity makes sensitivity quantification impracticable; casualty reserves face greater uncertainty from long settlement periods, inflation, legal and mass-tort risks. A 5% casualty liability increase is reasonably possible, implying about $1.8 billion higher liabilities and lower pretax earnings, but is not a worst-case estimate.

nodes.title: Retroactive reinsurance
nodes.summary: Retroactive reinsurance covers losses from events before contract inception, mainly long-tail casualty and liability claims. At December 31, 2025, gross unpaid losses were $31.0 billion; aggregate remaining payments are expected not to exceed $46 billion, and losses are considered unlikely to reach that limit or vary by more than 15% from estimated gross liabilities. Estimates use contract-level exposure, trends, payment history, scenarios, and ongoing claims information, with reassessment when circumstances change. Asbestos and environmental liabilities were $11.1 billion; limited claims data and legal, regulatory, and judicial developments create uncertainty. Prior-year ultimate liabilities rose $261 million in 2025, with insignificant underwriting impact after deferred-charge changes. Deferred-charge assets were $8.1 billion and are expected to fall about $800 million in 2026, reducing pretax earnings correspondingly.

nodes.title: Other Critical Accounting Estimates
nodes.summary: At December 31, 2025, the company reported $83.1 billion in goodwill and $18.9 billion in indefinite-lived intangible assets, tested annually and when circumstances suggest possible impairment. Valuations use methods such as market data, earnings multiples, and discounted cash flows, relying on forecasts and other assumptions subject to significant judgment and uncertainty. Carrying values above fair value result in impairment charges (for goodwill, capped at its carrying amount). Goodwill was assessed as not impaired, but adverse market, economic, business, or industry changes could lead to future losses.

nodes.title: Other Critical Accounting Estimates

nodes.title: Definition and Limitations of Internal Control over Financial Reporting
nodes.summary: Internal control over financial reporting aims to provide reasonable assurance that external financial statements comply with generally accepted accounting principles. It includes policies and procedures for accurate records of transactions and asset dispositions; authorized recording of transactions, receipts, and expenditures; and prevention or timely detection of unauthorized asset use or disposition that could materially affect financial statements. Inherent limitations mean controls may not prevent or detect misstatements, and future effectiveness may decline due to changing conditions or reduced compliance.

nodes.title: Significant Accounting Policies and Practices
key_items: (a) Nature of operations and basis of consolidation
(b) Use of estimates in preparation of financial statements
(c) Cash and cash equivalents and short-term investments in U.S. Treasury Bills
nodes.summary: Berkshire is a diversified holding company; its consolidated statements include controlled subsidiaries and qualifying variable interest entities, with intercompany balances eliminated. Railroad, utilities and energy subsidiaries are presented separately because of their significant assets, capital spending and debt, and lack of Berkshire financial support. GAAP statements use estimates subject to uncertainty and future revision, particularly for insurance claims, reinsurance, fair values, impairment and credit losses; actual results may differ. Cash equivalents have purchase-date maturities of three months or less, while short-term Treasury Bills mature in more than three months but less than one year.

nodes.title: (d) Investments in fixed maturity securities
nodes.summary: The text explains accounting policies for fixed maturity securities, equity securities, equity-method investments, and loans. Fixed maturities are classified as held-to-maturity, trading, or available-for-sale, with corresponding amortized-cost or fair-value treatment, interest-method amortization, and rules for realized gains, impairment, and credit-loss allowances. Equity securities are fair-valued through earnings. Equity-method accounting covers significant influence, qualifying investments, carrying-value changes, distributions, losses, and disposals. Loans are generally held at amortized cost with expected-credit-loss allowances; costs and fees adjust yield, loss estimates incorporate historical, current, and forecast factors, and delinquency, nonaccrual, interest reversal, and accrual-resumption rules are specified.

nodes.title: Investment Accounting Policies
nodes.summary: Available-for-sale fixed maturity securities generate gains or losses in earnings upon sale; unrealized losses are recognized as credit losses in earnings when applicable, while noncredit losses go to accumulated other comprehensive income, with allowances adjusted as circumstances change. Equity securities are measured at fair value, with changes in earnings. The equity method applies to qualifying significant-influence investments (generally over 20% voting interest), subject to exceptions; carrying values reflect the investor’s share of earnings, losses, and comprehensive income, added investments, and distributions. Certain losses may continue after carrying value reaches zero, and disposal gains or losses enter earnings.

nodes.title: (g) Loans and finance receivables
nodes.summary: Loans and finance receivables are mainly manufactured-home loans, carried at amortized cost less expected-credit-loss allowances; related costs, fees, premiums and discounts adjust yield. Credit-loss estimates consider loan performance, historical and forecast factors, collateral and modified cash flows. Delinquency, nonaccrual, foreclosure, interest recognition and charge-off policies are described. Other receivables, including reinsurance recoverables, are allowance-adjusted using credit history, forecasts and counterparty protections, and charged off after collection efforts. Fair value principles address market conditions, valuation judgment and liability credit risk. Inventories use LIFO for 30% and other cost methods, with non-LIFO lower of cost or net realizable value. Property and leased equipment are capitalized at cost, including qualifying construction costs; routine maintenance is expensed.

nodes.title: Receivables, Fair Value, and Inventory Policies
nodes.summary: Other receivables include customer, insurance, and reinsurance balances, reported net of expected credit loss allowances based on historical losses, current conditions, forecasts, counterparty quality, and credit enhancements; balances are charged off after collection efforts fail. Fair value reflects an orderly market-participant transaction, with adjustments or alternative techniques in illiquid markets, consideration of liability credit risk, and estimation uncertainty. Inventories include manufactured and resale goods, supplies, and homes; costs include production expenses. At year-end 2025, 30% used LIFO and most remaining inventory used FIFO or average cost; non-LIFO inventory is valued at lower of cost or net realizable value. LIFO replacement-cost excesses were $2.5 billion in 2025 and $2.3 billion in 2024.

nodes.title: (k) Property, plant and equipment and equipment held for lease
nodes.summary: The policy covers capitalization and expensing of property, plant, equipment, and leased equipment, including construction costs, qualifying indirect costs, and regulated-asset financing allowances. It explains depreciation methods, retirement and disposal accounting, and useful-life ranges for railroad, utility, energy, other-business, and leased assets. It also describes impairment reviews triggered by adverse changes or sale plans, recoverability testing using undiscounted cash flows and residual value, write-downs to fair value, and special consideration of regulation for utility and energy subsidiaries.

nodes.title: (l) Leases
nodes.summary: The company leases property and recognizes right-of-use assets and lease liabilities for its right to use leased assets and make payments. Payments include fixed amounts and index- or rate-based variable amounts; the lease term is the non-cancellable period. Renewal options are included only when exercise is reasonably certain, while performance- or usage-based variable payments may also apply. Liabilities are generally measured using incremental borrowing rates, and right-of-use assets are reviewed for impairment. The company elects not to separate lease and non-lease components for some asset classes and does not recognize assets or liabilities for leases of one year or less.

nodes.title: (m) Goodwill and other intangible assets
nodes.summary: Goodwill is the excess of a business’s acquisition price over the acquisition-date value of its identifiable net assets and is tested for impairment at least annually. Reporting-unit fair value is estimated using methods such as market quotations, asset and liability values, discounted projected earnings or cash flows, and earnings multiples. Any carrying-value excess over fair value, up to the goodwill balance, is charged to earnings. Indefinite-lived intangible assets are tested annually and when impairment indicators arise, with any excess carrying value charged to earnings; these assessments require significant judgment. Finite-lived intangibles are amortized according to expected benefit consumption or straight-line over useful lives and reviewed for impairment when indicators suggest their carrying amount may not be recoverable.

nodes.title: (n) Revenue recognition
nodes.summary: Insurance premiums are recognized according to contract type: over coverage periods for prospective property/casualty contracts, at inception for retroactive reinsurance and periodic-payment annuities, and when due for life reinsurance; amounts are net of ceded premiums and reflect estimated experience. Sales and service revenue is recognized as customers obtain control, allocated among performance obligations by relative standalone prices, and adjusted for returns, discounts, penalties, incentives, and applicable taxes. Product sales are recognized at transfer, or over time for qualifying customized contracts. Freight revenue is recognized as transportation occurs, with incentives reducing revenue. Regulated utility revenue is recognized as energy is delivered or services provided, including billed and unbilled amounts, with estimated refunds accrued where needed. Other services are recognized over time or upon completion; leasing revenue is recognized over the lease term or by usage, mostly under operating leases.

nodes.title: (o) Losses and loss adjustment expenses (“losses and LAE”)
nodes.summary: The company records undiscounted estimated ultimate liabilities for unpaid insurance losses and loss adjustment expenses (LAE) from events occurring by the balance-sheet date. Estimates use policyholder and cedent reports, individual case estimates, and incurred-but-not-reported losses. Earnings include paid claims and settlement costs plus changes in unpaid estimates, net of reinsurance recoveries and amounts estimated recoverable. Reinsurance does not release the ceding company from its obligations to policyholders.

nodes.title: (p) Retroactive reinsurance
nodes.summary: The text describes accounting policies for retroactive reinsurance, including loss liabilities and deferred charges adjusted using the interest method; capitalization and amortization of insurance acquisition costs; measurement of long-duration life, annuity, and health benefit liabilities using cash-flow and discount-rate assumptions, with assumption changes in earnings and discount-rate changes in OCI; regulated-utility regulatory assets and liabilities and their recognition or write-off; and foreign-currency translation, with translation effects in OCI and transaction or remeasurement gains and losses in earnings.

nodes.title: Insurance Costs, Benefits, and Regulated Operations
key_items: (r) Life, annuity and health insurance benefits
nodes.summary: The notes explain that successful insurance acquisition costs are capitalized, with other underwriting costs expensed, and describe how deferred costs are amortized for short- and long-duration contracts. They outline how life, annuity, and health benefit liabilities are measured using expected cash flows, premiums, actuarial assumptions, and periodically updated discount rates, with assumption changes in earnings and discount-rate changes in other comprehensive income. Regulated utilities defer recoverable costs and accrued revenues as regulatory assets and liabilities, recognize them over future periods, and reassess whether recovery or return through rates remains probable.

nodes.title: (t) Foreign currency
nodes.summary: Foreign-currency financial statements are translated using average rates for revenues and expenses and period-end rates for assets and liabilities, with translation effects in accumulated other comprehensive income; transaction and remeasurement gains or losses enter earnings. Income-tax policies cover consolidated and jurisdictional filings, current and deferred taxes, tax-rate changes, valuation allowances, and uncertain positions, including interest and penalties. Berkshire adopted ASU 2023-09 retrospectively in 2025; ASU 2024-03, requiring expense-category disclosures, is effective after December 15, 2026, with early adoption allowed. Berkshire completed its approximately $9.5 billion acquisition of Occidental’s OxyChem on January 2, 2026; Occidental retained legacy environmental liabilities. Preliminary assets and liabilities are $10.8 billion and $1.3 billion, respectively; goodwill is expected to be immaterial, and no material financial-statement impact is anticipated.

nodes.title: Income Taxes and Accounting Pronouncements
key_items: (w) Accounting pronouncements to be adopted subsequent to December 31, 2025
nodes.summary: Berkshire files consolidated U.S. federal and other jurisdictional tax returns, accrues current and deferred taxes, accounts for deferred tax balances and rate changes, provides valuation allowances when needed, and records liabilities, interest, and penalties for uncertain tax positions. In 2025, it retrospectively adopted ASU 2023-09, enhancing income tax rate reconciliation and taxes-paid disclosures. ASU 2024-03 will require disaggregation of certain income statement expenses; it is effective for fiscal years beginning after December 15, 2026, with prospective or retrospective adoption and early adoption permitted.

They also cover tax accounting changes, new accounting standards, and the 2026 OxyChem acquisition.

nodes.title: (2) Significant business acquisitions
nodes.summary: Berkshire’s acquisition strategy targets businesses with consistent earnings, strong equity returns, and capable, honest management; acquired results enter consolidated statements from the acquisition date. On January 2, 2026, Berkshire acquired Occidental’s OxyChem for approximately $9.5 billion, subject to adjustment, with Occidental retaining legacy environmental liabilities. OxyChem makes basic chemicals for diverse industries. Asset and liability valuations remain preliminary at $10.8 billion and $1.3 billion; assets are expected to include property, receivables, inventory, equity-method investments, and intangibles. nodes.summary: Equity investments are concentrated: the five largest holdings—American Express, Apple, Bank of America, Coca-Cola and Chevron—accounted for 65% of fair value in 2025 and 71% in 2024. Occidental common shares use the equity method, while its preferred stock and warrants are carried at fair value. The preferred stock pays an 8% dividend, is redeemable from 2029 at 105% of liquidation value, and had $8.5 billion of liquidation value at year-end 2025, with about $1.5 billion redeemed. title: INSIDER TRADING POLICIES AND PROCEDURES

nodes.title: INSIDER TRADING POLICIES AND PROCEDURES (intro)
nodes.summary: Berkshire Hathaway’s insider trading policies explain that securities laws prohibit anyone with material nonpublic information from trading relevant publicly traded securities or tipping others. The rules cover Berkshire and its subsidiaries, as well as other companies, particularly those involved in Berkshire investments or contemplated transactions; employees generally must wait for relevant news to become public. Violations can bring civil and criminal penalties, while supervisors may face liability for failing to prevent others’ trading. Berkshire cooperates with regulators’ requests for employee information and applies these policies to covered persons and certain family members; violations may lead to discipline, including dismissal, regardless of legal penalties.

nodes.title: Definitions of Certain Terms
nodes.summary: Defines key terms in Berkshire Hathaway’s insider-trading policies: the Board, Clearing Officers and their recusal from clearing their own trades, Covered Employees, Covered Persons and their possible additional designees, Directors, and Family Members. “Material” information is investor-significant or price-affecting, with undisclosed Berkshire transactions in other companies presumed material; “nonpublic” information is not publicly available or not yet absorbed by the market. Permitted Trading covers approved Rule 10b5-1 plans, specified investment-manager arrangements, and independent discretionary trading designees who have not received relevant material nonpublic information. “Trading” includes securities purchases, sales, gifts, acquisition or disposal contracts, and options or other derivatives.

nodes.title: Policies
nodes.summary: Covered Persons may not trade or recommend trading Berkshire securities while holding material nonpublic information, or other companies’ securities when such information was learned through their Berkshire role or a relevant family member. This includes companies Berkshire has invested in, is considering investing in, may transact significantly with, or knows about through investor, counterparty, or board relationships. Unauthorized disclosure of such information is also prohibited; both traders and those who tip others may face civil and criminal charges. The text cites Rajat Gupta’s prison sentence, $13.9 million penalty, and ban from public-company leadership for disclosing confidential information about Berkshire’s planned Goldman Sachs investment.

nodes.title: Procedures
key_items: Insider Trading Policies and Procedures Page 4 of 5
nodes.summary: The procedures may be changed or supplemented by Berkshire. Directors and executive officers and their families must pre-clear Berkshire trades except permitted trades; other covered employees and families may trade without pre-clearance during the 45 days after quarterly or annual SEC filings if they lack material nonpublic information, and must pre-clear otherwise. Restrictions also govern trading in other companies’ securities when Berkshire positions or material transactions are known, being considered, publicly disclosed, or later ended; applicable pre-clearance continues until specified disclosures. Directors and covered employees must certify compliance quarterly. Pre-clearance does not remove legal insider-trading obligations, and approved trades must occur within five business days unless otherwise authorized. Directors and employees should return certifications and may direct questions to Berkshire’s CFO.
